elements.id-string-2: \title{Scalable Neural Contextual Bandit for Recommender Systems}
elements.id-string-11: High-quality recommender systems ought to deliver both innovative and relevant content through effective and exploratory interactions with users.
elements.id-string-12: Yet, supervised learning-based neural networks, which form the backbone of many existing recommender systems, only leverage recognized user interests, falling short when it comes to efficiently uncovering unknown user preferences.
elements.id-string-13: While there has been some progress with neural contextual bandit algorithms towards enabling online exploration through neural networks, their onerous computational demands hinder widespread adoption in real-world recommender systems.
elements.id-string-14: In this work, we propose a scalable sample-efficient neural contextual bandit algorithm for recommender systems.
elements.id-string-15: To do this, we design an epistemic neural network architecture, Epistemic Neural Recommendation (ENR), that enables Thompson sampling at a large scale.In two distinct large-scale experiments with real-world tasks, ENR significantly boosts click-through rates and user ratings by at least $9\%$ and $6\%$ respectively compared to state-of-the-art neural contextual bandit algorithms.
elements.id-string-16: Furthermore, it achieves equivalent performance with at least $29\%$ fewer user interactions compared to the best-performing baseline algorithm.
elements.id-string-17: Remarkably, while accomplishing these improvements, ENR demands orders of magnitude fewer computational resources than neural contextual bandit baseline algorithms.
elements.id-string-18: \keywords{Recommender Systems, Contextual Bandits, Reinforcement Learning, Exploration vs Exploitation, Decision Making under Uncertainty}

elements.id-string-22: Recommender systems (RS), paramount in personalizing digital content, critically influence the quality of information accessed via the Internet.
elements.id-string-23: Traditionally, these systems have employed supervised learning algorithms, such as Collaborative Filtering \cite{resnick1994grouplens}, which have greatly benefited from advances in deep learning.
elements.id-string-24: These algorithms analyze vast quantities of data to discern user preferences; however, they are not designed to strategically probe in order to more quickly learn about user interests.
elements.id-string-25: Instead, they learn passively from collected data.
elements.id-string-26: Current research \cite{jiang2019degenerate, salamo2005reducing, gravino2019towards} reveals that deep-learning-driven RS tend to quickly confine their focus to a limited set of suboptimal topics, limiting their scope and hampering their learning capacity.
elements.id-string-27: This restrictive personalization strategy confines RS to recommend only those topics with which they have established familiarity, thus failing to discover and learn users' other potential interests.
elements.id-string-28: The ability of an RS to identify and learn about user's unexplored interests is a significant determinant of its long-term performance.
elements.id-string-29: The concept of exploration in RS draws heavily from bandit learning \cite{slivkins2019introduction}.
elements.id-string-30: In the bandit learning formulation of RS, the system functions as an agent, each user represents a unique context, and each recommendation is an action.
elements.id-string-31: Bandit learning algorithms, such as upper confidence bound (UCB) \cite{agrawal1995sample, auer2002finite} and Thompson sampling \cite{thompson1933likelihood}, provide the groundwork for efficient exploration.
elements.id-string-32: Theoretical advances \cite{agrawal2012analysis, dong2018information, dong2019performance, auer2002using, agrawal1995sample, auer2002finite} have offered great insight into these methods, and the efficacy of such methods has been demonstrated through experiments with small-scale environments.
elements.id-string-33: While much of this literature has focused on small-scale environments that do not require that an agent generalizes across contexts and actions, the scale of practical RS calls for such generalization.
elements.id-string-34: Advances in neural bandits offer flexible and scalable approaches to generalization that support more sample-efficient exploration algorithms.
elements.id-string-35: Building on ideas developed for linear UCB and linear Thompson sampling \cite{li2010contextual, chapelle2011empirical}, these approaches offer variations of UCB and Thompson sampling that interoperate with deep learning \cite{li2010contextual, zhou2020neural, xu2021neural,abeille2017linear, zhang2021neural, lu2017ensemble,dwaracherla2019hypermodels,OsbandNeuralTestbed,QinEnsembleSampling}.
elements.id-string-36: While these approaches may be sample-efficient, their computational requirements become onerous at scale.
elements.id-string-37: This has limited their practical impact.
elements.id-string-38: An obstacle to scaling aforementioned approaches has been in the computation required to maintain and apply epistemic uncertainty estimates.
elements.id-string-39: Such estimates allow an agent to {\it know what it does not know}, which is critical for guiding exploration.
elements.id-string-40: The EpiNet \cite{osband2021epistemic} offers a scalable approach to uncertainty estimation, and therefore, a path toward supporting efficient exploration in practical RS.
elements.id-string-41: In particular, epinet-enhanced deep learning combined with Thompson sampling, has the potential to greatly improve RS' exploration capabilities and therefore improve personalization.
elements.id-string-42: To this end, we introduce Epistemic Neural Recommendation (ENR), a novel architecture customized for RS.
elements.id-string-43: We run a series of experiments using large-scale real-world RS datasets to empirically demonstrate that ENR outperforms state-of-the-art neural contextual bandit algorithms.
elements.id-string-44: ENR greatly enhances personalization, achieving an $9\%$ and $6\%$ improvement in click-through rate and user rating, respectively, across two real-world experiments.
elements.id-string-45: Furthermore, it attains the performance of the best baseline algorithm with at least $20\%$ fewer user interactions.
elements.id-string-46: Importantly, ENR accomplishes these while requiring orders of magnitude fewer computational resources than neural contextual bandit baseline algorithms, making it a considerably more scalable solution.
elements.id-string-47: As a spoiler, please see Figure \ref{fig:mind_tradeoff} for a computation-performance tradeoff comparison between our method and baseline methods based on one of our real-world experiments.
elements.id-string-48: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
elements.id-string-49: In Section 2, we formulate RS as a contextual bandit.
elements.id-string-50: In Section 3, we review existing online contextual bandit algorithms, current industry adoptions, and their relative merits.
elements.id-string-51: In Section 4, we introduce Epistemic Neural Recommendation.
elements.id-string-52: In Section 5, we present empirical results.
elements.id-string-53: In Section 6, we summarize our contributions, benefits they afford, and potential future directions for neural contextual bandits.
elements.id-string-55: We conceptualize the design of RS as a contextual bandit problem where an agent interacts with a RS environment by taking an action (recommendation) based on a context (user) observed.
elements.id-string-56: More formally, the environment $\mathcal{E}$ is specified by a triple that consists of an observation space $\mathcal{O}$, an action space $\mathcal{A}$, and an observation probability function $P_O$.
elements.id-string-57: \textbf{Observation space $\mathcal{O}$}: In a contextual bandit problem, the observation generated by the environment offers feedback in response to the previous action taken by the agent as well as a new context the agent needs to execute an action.
elements.id-string-58: Formally, $\mathcal{O} = \mathcal{S} \times \mathbb{R}$ and at time step $t$, $O_t = (S_t, R_t)$.
elements.id-string-60: This context could, for example, provide a user's demographic information as well as data from their past interactions.
elements.id-string-61: We will sometimes refer to $S_t$ as a user, since we think of it as providing information that distinguishes users.
elements.id-string-62: $R_t \in \mathbb{R}$ denotes scalar feedback from the user of the previous time step $t-1$ in response to the action $A_{t-1}$.
elements.id-string-63: For example, $R_t$ could be binary-valued, indicating whether the user clicked in response to a recommendation.
elements.id-string-64: We will refer to $R_t$ as the reward received by the agent at time $t$.
elements.id-string-65: \textbf{Action space $\mathcal{A}$}: At each time $t$, the agent selects an action $A_{t} \in \mathcal{A}$, which identifies a content unit for recommendation to the user $S_t$.
elements.id-string-66: The action space $\mathcal{A}$ specifies the range of possibilities afforded by the universe of available content.
elements.id-string-67: \textbf{Observation probability function $P_O$}: The observation probability function assigns a probability $P_O(O_{t+1}|S_t,A_t)$ to each possible outcome $O_{t+1} = (S_{t+1}, R_{t+1})$ from recommending $A_t$ to user $S_t$.
elements.id-string-68: This probability is a product of two others, specified by functions $P_S$ and $P_R$:
elements.id-string-70: \begin{equation} P_O(O_{t+1} | S_t, A_t) = P_S(S_{t+1})P_{R}(R_{t+1} | S_t, A_t). \vspace{-5pt} \end{equation}
elements.id-string-71: $P_S$ provides context probabilities, and $P_R$ provides reward probabilities.
elements.id-string-72: At time $t$, the environment samples a new user $S_t \sim P_S$.
elements.id-string-73: The agent then supplies a recommendation $A_t$, and the environment samples $R_{t+1} \sim P_{R}(\cdot| S_t, A_t)$.
elements.id-string-74: The overall objective of the agent is to maximize its average reward $\frac{1}{T}\sum^T_{t=1} R_t$ over $T$ time steps.
elements.id-string-75: Note that, though each action $A_t$ does not directly impact any user other than $S_t$, the action influences what information is gathered through the observation $R_{t+1}$.
elements.id-string-76: As such, the action bears an indirect impact on subequent users through what the agent learns, which can improve its ability to make useful recommendations.
elements.id-string-77: Optimizing the delayed benefits of learning requires strategic sequential decisions that balance exploration versus exploitation.
elements.id-string-78: We think of $S_t$ and $A_t$ as offering information about users and content units in arbitrary raw formats.
elements.id-string-79: Agents, however, often rely on starting with a more structured representations provided by domain experts.
elements.id-string-80: In this work, we also assume availability of feature extractors that map $S_t$ and $A_t$ to such representations $\phi_{A_t}$ and $\psi_{S_t}$.
elements.id-string-81: Note that our problem formulation encompasses only online learning.
elements.id-string-82: In a real RS, one would pretrain an agent offline on historical data before engaging in online learning.
elements.id-string-83: The methods we develop for online learning can be applied in this workflow post pretraining of an epinet-enhanced model.
elements.id-string-84: However, in order to focus our attention on the problem of exploration, in this paper, we limit our discussions, designs and experiments to the online learning part and leave offline learning for future work.
elements.id-string-86: Among various bandit algorithms, there are two most commonly adopted online bandit strategies.
elements.id-string-87: One explores based on the reward estimates sampled from context-action pairs' posterior distributions, represented by Thompson sampling \cite{thompson1933likelihood}, and the other follows the "optimism in the face of uncertainty" principle, represented by upper confidence bound (UCB) \cite{agrawal1995sample, auer2002finite}.
elements.id-string-88: In this section, we offer a high level introduction to Thompson sampling and UCB algorithms as well as their extensions to contextual settings.
elements.id-string-89: The deep neural network versions of the algorithms are considered baselines for our work.
elements.id-string-90: We will also review related industry and practical adoptions of these strategies.
elements.id-string-91: Thompson Sampling, Its Extensions and Related Adoptions
elements.id-string-92: Thompson sampling is an exploration strategy that samples reward estimates from context-action pairs' posterior distributions and then executes greedily with respect to these samples.
elements.id-string-93: This strategy is particularly popular due to its simplicity.
elements.id-string-94: Following the definition in Section \ref{sec:prob}, we first consider a vanilla Thompson sampling algorithm \cite{thompson1933likelihood} for multi-armed bandits.
elements.id-string-95: For a multi-armed bandit, the context $S_t$ is always the same and the agent needs to choose $A_t$ from $\mathcal{A}$ without any representation learning.
elements.id-string-96: A Thompson sampling agent keeps a reward posterior distribution $\hat{P}_{a}$ for each arm $a$ and updates it over time.

elements.id-string-100: The agent then updates its posterior belief $\hat{P}_{a}$ with the latest reward $R_{t+1}$ and selected action $A_t$.
elements.id-string-101: The vanilla Thompson sampling approach is a popular production strategy when it comes to small action space recommendations \cite{sanz2019simple, hsieh2015efficient}.
elements.id-string-102: Extending Thompson sampling to large action space and contextual bandits, an agent can compute parametric estimates of rewards of context-action pairs by sampling linear model parameters from the posterior belief \cite{abeille2017linear, agrawal2013thompson,russo2013eluder,russo2014posterior,russo2018tutorial} instead of sampling a point estimate from the reward posterior distribution.
elements.id-string-103: Here, a linear Thompson sampling agent keeps track of a posterior belief $\hat{P}_\theta$ over the parameters $\theta$.
elements.id-string-106: The agent then updates its posterior belief of $\hat{P}_\theta$ with the latest reward $R_{t+1}$, context $S_t$ and action $A_t$.
elements.id-string-107: The posterior update could be performed via Laplace approximation \cite{laplace1986memoir}, and is also presented in industry adoptions of linear Thompson sampling \cite{chapelle2011empirical}.
elements.id-string-108: The method above could be extended to neural networks as the agent can also keep a posterior belief over neural network parameters.
elements.id-string-109: To avoid heavy computation of Laplace approximation, various Bayesian methods have been proposed to achieve posterior updates for distributions over neural network parameters, including deep ensemble \cite{lakshminarayanan2017simple}, ensemble sampling with prior networks \cite{lu2017ensemble}, Bayes by Backprop \cite{blundell2015weight}, Hypermodels \cite{dwaracherla2019hypermodels}, Monte-Carlo Dropouts \cite{gal2016dropout} and EpiNet \cite{osband2021epistemic}.
elements.id-string-110: Among the methods above, the two ensemble methods \cite{broden2018ensemble, lu2018efficient, tang2014ensemble} and Monte-Carlo Dropout \cite{guo2020deep} are the most commonly adopted methods for contextual bandits with parameter posterior sampling in a practical setting.
elements.id-string-111: One additional line of work that leverages Thompson sampling for neural networks is neural Thompson sampling \cite{zhang2021neural}.
elements.id-string-112: In this approach, instead of sampling from parameters' posterior distribution, neural Thompson sampling directly samples from the posterior estimate of the reward of a context-action pair.

elements.id-string-148: In this section, we introduce a novel architecture for scalable neural contextual bandit problems, drawing inspiration from Thompson sampling and recent developments in epistemic neural networks (ENN) and EpiNet \cite{osband2021epistemic}.
elements.id-string-149: As discussed in Section \ref{sec:ts}, the objective of a deep learning-based Thompson sampling strategy is to accurately estimate the uncertainty of a prediction, pertaining to a context-action pair, while keeping computational costs to a minimum.
elements.id-string-150: A significant drawback of many neural methods for Thompson sampling and UCB is their computationally expensive uncertainty estimation process, which impedes their integration into real-world environments.
elements.id-string-151: The primary aim of our proposed architecture and design is to address this very issue, while enhancing model performance.
elements.id-string-153: A key aspect shared across all neural exploration methods is the generation of effective representations for context-action pairs.
elements.id-string-154: Within the contextual bandit framework, there are three main representation factors to consider: action representation, context representation, and the interaction between context and action.
elements.id-string-155: We assume a general and unnormalized feature representation from the environment for both contexts and actions.
elements.id-string-156: To distill both context and action feature representation vectors, we initially feed each vector into a linear layer followed by a ReLU activation function.
elements.id-string-157: This is subsequently followed by a Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) layer \cite{ba2016layer}.
elements.id-string-158: Given that raw features can contain disproportionately large values that are challenging to normalize - particularly in an online bandit setting where data continually stream in - it is crucial to employ layer normalization.
elements.id-string-159: This technique ensures smoother gradients, promoting stability and generalizability \cite{xu2019understanding}.

elements.id-string-163: Note that after summarization through these two layers, the outputs are of the same shape.

elements.id-string-176: Using the representation derived above, we can now design a neural network for both point estimate and uncertainty estimation.
elements.id-string-177: For efficient epistemic uncertainty estimation using neural networks, we employ EpiNet \cite{osband2021epistemic}, an auxiliary architecture for a general neural network.
elements.id-string-178: This architecture leverages the final layer representation of a neural network, along with an epistemic index $z$, to generate a sample from the posterior.
elements.id-string-179: EpiNet presents a cost-effective method for constructing ENNs, which has been demonstrated to excel in making joint predictions for classification and supervised learning tasks, while achieving strong performance in synthesized neural logistic bandits with minimal additional computational costs.
elements.id-string-180: However, a drawback of only utilizing the last layer representation, particularly in a contextual bandit setting, is the diminished representation power.
elements.id-string-181: The interactions between context and action are summarized through multi-layers perceptrons for marginal predictions, and considerable information is lost in the process.
elements.id-string-182: Motivated by this, we introduce Epistemic Neural Recommendation (ENR) that generates improved posterior samples via more informative representations.
elements.id-string-183: The remaining architecture of ENR is comprised of three parts: a function $f_{\theta_x}: \mathbb{R}^{3d_E} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ for marginal prediction, and two functions $g_{\sigma}$ and $g_{\sigma^p}$, both mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{3d_E}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d_z}$, for uncertainty estimation.
elements.id-string-184: Upon extraction of $x_{t, A}$, we employ $f_{\theta_x}$ to make the marginal prediction via $f_{\theta_x}(x_{t,A})$.
elements.id-string-185: In addition to $f_{\theta_x}$, $g_{\sigma}$ and $g_{\sigma^p}$ are independently initialized through Glorot Initialization \cite{glorot2010understanding, bartlett2017spectrally}, and $g_{\sigma^p}$ remains constant throughout its lifetime, thereby providing robust regularization.
elements.id-string-186: To initialize this segment of the network, ENR samples an epistemic index $z$ from its prior $P_z$, which could either be a discrete one-hot vector or a standard multivariate Gaussian sample.
elements.id-string-187: The sampled $z$ is then concatenated with $x_{t, A}$ and processed through both $g_{\sigma}$ and $g_{\sigma^p}$.
elements.id-string-188: Consequently, the uncertainty estimation is $(g_{\sigma}(x_{t, A}, z) + g_{\sigma^p}(x_{t, A}, z))^T z$.
elements.id-string-189: Hence the final output of ENR is

elements.id-string-299: MIND is a large-scale dataset generated by Microsoft news recommender system.
elements.id-string-300: It provides anonymized data logs that record each user's historical interesting articles and their impression as well as click logs with new recommendations.
elements.id-string-301: The dataset contains over millions of anonymized interaction logs.
elements.id-string-302: For statistics of the dataset, please refer to Table \ref{tab:stats}.
elements.id-string-303: One unique advantage of the MIND dataset for contextual bandit setup is its complete ground truth.
elements.id-string-304: At time step $t$, the MIND dataset logs $K$ distinct news recommendations sent to the user and records the news articles the user gave good feedback on, all of which happen at a single timestamp.
elements.id-string-305: Please see Table \ref{tab:mind_example} for an illustration of the data we use.
elements.id-string-306: Hence when evaluating the outcome of any action chosen by an agent among the sent recommendations, we can directly use the groundtruth from the dataset and avoid counterfactual evaluation which leads to high variance.
elements.id-string-307: In this experiment, we use all exploration baseline strategies as well as NCF \cite{he2017neural}, NAML \cite{wu2019naml} and NRMS \cite{wu2019neural} for neural network architecture baselines.

elements.id-string-352: From the results, we can see that ENR outperforms all other candidates in both in-sample online interactions as well as offline out-of-sample evaluation set by $4\%$ and $6\%$ respectively.
elements.id-string-353: Another observation we draw from the result is that with a complete action space provided to the agent at every timestep, all algorithms significantly improve in generalization capabilities from in-sample predictions to out-of-sample predictions.

elements.id-string-356: In this section, we cover some ablation studies regarding some of our hyperparameter choices as well as some design choices.
elements.id-string-359: In ENR, one of a key components for action and context summarization is Layer Normalization.
elements.id-string-360: As ENR is designed to take in any context and action inputs, it is common to observe a few features that are outsized.
elements.id-string-361: To ensure that context action interaction is not dominated by a few particular features, before the item-wise multiplication, we add a Layer Normalization operator to ensure more stability in the neural network as well as getting less impacted by outliers during training.
elements.id-string-362: See Figure \ref{fig:layernorm} for a performance comparison between ENR with and without Layer Normalization.
elements.id-string-364: Epistemic index $z$ is the key to identify a posterior sample from an ENR, and we study the impact of index dimension in this study.
elements.id-string-366: As the width of the index grows, the performance of the algorithm relatively decays.
elements.id-string-367: From the figure, we can also see that index width of 5 outperforms others.
elements.id-string-368: Hence we choose 5 for all of our experiments.
elements.id-string-369: Selection of ENR Uncertainty Prior Network Scale
elements.id-string-370: The prior network is a key means to regularize Epistemic Neural Networks by pulling the posterior distribution back from diverging too far away from the prior distribution to avoid distribution collapse.
elements.id-string-371: We study the prior network scale for ENR through a sweep.
elements.id-string-372: Note that prior scale is a scalar ranging $(0, 1)$.
elements.id-string-374: We see that setting prior scale to 0.3 offers the best performance.
elements.id-string-376: In this paper, we designed a scalable and novel neural contextual bandit algorithm customized for recommender systems via a new epistemic neural network architecture and Thompson sampling.
elements.id-string-377: We formally define the recommender system problem as a contextual bandit problem and reviewed the current State-of-the-Art neural contextual bandit strategies.
elements.id-string-378: Our architecture design, Epistemic Neural Recommendation (ENR), presents much better scalability compared to other neural contextual bandit strategies.
elements.id-string-379: We show empirically through both synthetic experiments as well as two large-scale real-world experiments that ENR outperforms all other baselines.
